The difference between cars and guns is that cars are created with a primary purpose of transport, socializing, commerce, etc. Of safety moving people and things from point A to point B in a spread out society. You have to either have a clear accident, or intentionally misuse them to overcome all the efforts at safety and end up causing an injury or fatality. No part of a vehicle is designed to kill intentionally. Quite the opposite. Because of the aforementioned overwhelming primary purpose of safely moving people and/or goods around in our society, we decide that the risk is an acceptable one balanced out by the overwhelming positive aspects of every day use.

Guns, on the other hand, are created to kill. Easily, quickly, repeatedly, accurately, at a distance. This is essentially their only purpose and any other purpose is only to emulate or practice this purpose.

Pretending the two have anything in common is disingenuous or just poorly reasoned.

Now of course we can still look at that same kind of risk assessment and decide whether or not the associated body count is worth the price for perceived personal freedom, a particular type of personal self defense, etc... but we have to be honest up front that the things being weighed are very different.

Finally, banning guns outright is generally not the issue for most people, but rather simply more effective reasonable regulation. But even if we were speaking of banning outright, even that would be a fundamentally different issue than banning cars (for reasons touched on above). We're not even in the same zip code of discussion when it comes to any sort of intellectually honest assessment of the issue of banning these two fundamentally different things. (And I do understand that some people realize that we're only talking about regulation, but believe that this would result in a slippery slope to eventual bans, but that is different than talking about bans right off the bat. I have more respect for people who rationally and honestly voice their concern about the slippery slope rather than creating the up front straw man of "ban guns!" any time reasonable regulation is brought up. Just a side note for clarification. I respect the slippery slope argument. I don't respect people who act like any mention of regulation is no different than calling for banning guns outright.)
The same argument could be made that guns are filling an inportant need in our society to defend and are only misued when appropriated for attack purposes.

As I said, one could make that argument, and we'd have to way that supposed need against the very real cost in human lives that is associated with it.

We could start by looking at the actual level of risk a person faces. Not what they feel, but the actual comparative risk to other crimes, fatality risks, etc. And then consider the reality that means reduction (restricting access to methods of harm) reduces things like suicides (which account for 2/3 of gun deaths annually in the US), and that even if criminals moved to other weapons, they are in general far less lethal, thus further reducing annual fatalities.

So again, it's a very different issue when you're claiming that guns are necessary to protect us from supposed existential threats, rather than being a daily requirement for easy transportation to and from work, school, to get to and from social events at various places, all things necessary for a healthy and functioning society and economy on a large scale etc.

Guns are for the most part something people get to feel safe, irrespective of whether or not that actually makes them more safe in reality. They are almost never used on a daily basis, and many, outside of practice, are never used at all for their intended purpose... while many are instead used for suicides, domestic violence, escalate situations that would not have otherwise escalated, or are stolen and fall into the hands of criminals where they then are used for violence etc...

Again, acting like there is any real parallel between the two in designed purpose, intended usage, daily use, relative risk, etc is absurd.

Of course we can have the discussion about how necessary widespread easy access to highly lethal killing machines designed only for that singular purpose is... but we cannot, with any shred of intellectual honesty, pretend it's the same argument as whether or not cars should be allowed because they can also be used to kill.
